title: Written methods
examples: Can you show me how to add these big numbers?
What is the best way to divide a large number?
If I have a remainder, what does that mean?

explain.say: Today we learn ways to write maths problems. We will use columns for adding and subtracting. Remember to line up your numbers neatly.
To add, you start from the ones column first. You add the digits in that column together. Then you carry any extra tens to the next column.

items: Add the digits in the ones column
Carry extra tens to the next column

explain.say: For subtraction, you start from the right side. If the top number is smaller, you need to borrow from the next column over. This is called regrouping.

items: Borrow if top number is smaller

explain.say: Long multiplication means multiplying by two or more numbers. You multiply the top number by each digit of the bottom number separately. Then you add the results.

items: Multiply top number by each digit

explain.say: Long division helps us share equally. You divide the bigger number by the smaller number. You write down how many times it fits inside. You then find the remainder.

faq.q: What is the difference between a remainder and a divisor?
faq.a: The divisor is the number you are dividing by. The remainder is what is left over after you have divided as much as possible.
asks: What does the remainder tell us?

faq.q: Do I always have to line up my numbers in columns?
faq.a: Yes, lining them up keeps the ones, tens, and hundreds correct. This is very important for adding and subtracting.

faq.q: When do I need to borrow in subtraction?
faq.a: You borrow when the digit on the top number is smaller than the digit on the bottom number. You take one ten from the column left.
asks: Can I borrow from the next column?

faq.q: Is long multiplication always harder than simple times tables?
faq.a: It takes more steps, but it is just repeated multiplication. You multiply by each digit one at a time.
asks: Is this just times tables in a long way?
Do I do it row by row?

faq.q: If I get a remainder, does it mean I made a mistake?
faq.a: No, a remainder just means the sharing was not perfectly even. It tells you how many items are left over.
asks: What do I do with the remainder?

facts: When adding or subtracting, always start with the ones column.
In long multiplication, you multiply by each digit separately.
Division tells us how many equal groups we can make.
A remainder is the amount left after dividing.

quiz.say: What is the first step when adding 345 plus 213?
quiz.why: You must always start adding from the rightmost column, which is the ones.

wrong.0: This is tempting because it is fast, but you must line up the place values correctly.
wrong.2: This is tempting because hundreds are the biggest numbers, but you must start with the ones.
wrong.3: This is tempting because the tens look big, but the ones column must always come first.

quiz.say: If you subtract 62 from 91, what is the first step?
quiz.why: Since one is smaller than two, you must borrow one ten from the nine. Then you subtract.

wrong.0: This is tempting because it is the right column, but you cannot subtract a bigger number from a smaller one.
wrong.1: This is tempting because the tens are bigger, but you must always start from the ones column.
wrong.3: This is tempting because you are working on the tens, but you must start with the ones column.

quiz.say: When dividing 25 by 4, what is the remainder?
quiz.why: Four goes into twenty-five six times, and there is one left over.

wrong.0: This is tempting because you might subtract 2 instead of 1 at the end.
wrong.2: This is tempting because 24 is a multiple of 4, but 25 is one more than 24.
wrong.3: This is tempting because you might stop when you get to 24, but you must account for the extra one.
